standard.title: Perfect Squares and Square Roots
standard.description: describe the relationship between perfect square numbers and square roots, and use squares of numbers and square roots of perfect square numbers to solve problems
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can multiply and divide whole numbers fluently, use arrays to represent multiplication, and understand that area of a square = side × side (from Y6 measurement and number work).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the relationship between perfect square numbers and their square roots, and apply this relationship to solve problems including finding the perimeter of squares given area.

nodes.label: Squares as area models
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can connect squaring a number to the area of a square with that side length, and list perfect square numbers from 1 to 144.
nodes.minimum_width: List perfect squares 1–144 and represent at least three using area diagrams.
nodes.typical_width: List perfect squares 1–400, connect each to its area diagram, and identify patterns in the sequence (e.g. differences between consecutive squares).
wider: Investigate the last-digit pattern in perfect squares (last digits cycle: 0,1,4,9,6,5,6,9,4,1,0) and use this to quickly rule out non-perfect-squares.
Explore why perfect squares always have an odd number of factors, connecting to divisibility.

response_modes.reason: Students need automatic recall of perfect squares to 144 before the square root relationship is legible. Fluency here is prerequisite to node 2.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack automatic recall of perfect squares to 144 cannot access the inverse relationship in Node 2 — the square root concept is not legible without the forward mapping being secure.
success_criteria: Lists perfect square numbers from 1² to 12² without error.
Represents a given perfect square as an area model and states its side length.
Does not confuse the square number with its root (e.g. does not say '9 squared is 3').

nodes.label: Square root as inverse operation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students understand that square root is the inverse of squaring and can find the exact square root of any perfect square up to 144.
nodes.minimum_width: Find the square root of any perfect square from 1 to 144 and explain what it means.
nodes.typical_width: Use √ notation fluently, explain the inverse relationship, and verify: √(n²) = n for concrete examples.
wider: Explore perfect squares beyond 144 (e.g. 169, 196, 225) using the area model and extend the pattern.
Investigate √(a × b) = √a × √b for perfect square cases (e.g. √36 = √4 × √9), building intuition without formalising the rule.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly confuse squaring with doubling (thinking 5² = 10) or treat √ as halving. Multiple concrete representations — area diagrams, calculator verification, number line — help resolve this.

nodes.hinge_reason: The squaring/doubling and √/halving misconceptions, if unresolved, produce systematic errors in Node 3 (bounding non-perfect squares) and Node 4 (applied problems) — students cannot reason about intervals or side lengths if the inverse relationship is confused.
success_criteria: States the square root of any perfect square from 1 to 144 when prompted.
Explains in words what √25 means ('the number that when multiplied by itself gives 25').
Does not conflate squaring with multiplying by 2.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The inverse relationship and its extension beyond 144 offer advancing students a foundation for irrational number intuition — exploring which numbers are perfect squares and which are not is rich structural thinking.

nodes.label: Locating non-perfect square roots
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify which two consecutive integers a square root falls between for numbers that are not perfect squares.
nodes.minimum_width: For a given non-perfect-square (e.g. 43), identify the two consecutive perfect squares it lies between and state the corresponding root interval.
nodes.typical_width: Estimate √n to one decimal place for non-perfect squares by reasoning about the interval, e.g. √43 ≈ 6.5.
wider: Use a number line marked with perfect squares to plot approximate positions of several non-perfect square roots.
Investigate: between which perfect squares does √200 fall? Extend to three-digit numbers.

response_modes.reason: Students need an explicit reasoning scaffold: 'find the perfect squares either side, take their roots, the answer lies between'. Without this structure students often guess randomly or over-rely on a calculator without understanding the bounds.

success_criteria: For any given number, correctly identifies the two consecutive perfect squares it lies between.
States the corresponding square root interval (e.g. '√43 is between 6 and 7').
Explains the reasoning, not just the answer.

nodes.label: Applying square roots to problems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use the relationship between perfect square numbers and square roots to solve practical problems, including finding the side length of a square given its area.
nodes.minimum_width: Given the area of a square, find its side length and perimeter using square root reasoning.
nodes.typical_width: Solve a range of problems involving squares and square roots in practical contexts (tile layouts, garden beds, square frames) including problems requiring identification of perfect square areas.
wider: Design a problem involving square tiles covering a floor area that requires checking whether a given area is a perfect square.
Connect to Pythagoras preparation: identify whether a² + b² is a perfect square for simple triples (3,4,5).

response_modes.reason: The transition from abstract square root to applied problem-solving requires varied contexts — students who only practise decontextualised calculations often fail to recognise when square root is the required operation in a problem.
This node connects squaring, square roots, area, and perimeter simultaneously — coordinating these is the learning.

success_criteria: Given the area of a square, correctly determines the side length using square root reasoning.
Solves a two-step problem involving squares and square roots in a practical context.
Checks that their answer is reasonable (e.g. side length must be positive).
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Applying square roots to multi-step practical problems (tiling, Pythagorean triples) connects number to geometry in ways that are rich and within Year 7 scope.
